2.text: a very large measure. The trouble is, however, that the fish cannot be

3.text: preserved in good condition for too long a time. Therefore, when a famine

4.text: comes, it happens too often that the fish-stores are either gone or quite putrid

5.text: and not fit for use. In cases of great need, the Administration distributes among

6.text: the starving population some of the rye-flour from the storehouses of the Crown.

7.text: This is given as a loan, which is to be covered afterwards, and the heavy

8.text: official price paid in full. In some years this is as high as fourteen rubles

9.text: per pud (twenty cents in American money per pound Avoirdupois). All this

10.text: (i.e., fish and flour), however, falls to the share only of the Russian creoles

11.text: and the Russianized natives. The others, especially those that dwell too far

12.text: from Russian towns, receive no succor, and are not rarely reduced to death

13.text: by starvation and to cannibalism. I am informed that in the last few years,

14.text: when fishing on the Kolyma has not been fairly successful, cases of starvation

15.text: and cannibalism among the Tungus and Yukaghir have happened quite

16.text: frequently. The latter tribe is dwindling away quite perceptibly.

17.text: The Chukchee, who for the most part pay no tribute, have no right to

18.text: official assistance, but it seems they do not feel themselves much the worse

19.text: for that. I mentioned before a Russian creole who grew up among the

20.text: Chukchee and lived the same life as they do in a nomadic camp, and with

21.text: a herd of reindeer. His name was Alexis Kasanov. Still, being a Russian

22.text: creole, and moreover a member of the Russian community on the Lower

23.text: Kolyma, which is burdened to the utmost with taxes, collections, and requisitions,

24.text: he had to bear a goodly share of all these payments. When he was in

25.text: arrears, his fellow-citizens contrived to seize him at the Anui fair or in

26.text: Nishne-Kolymsk; and he was released only after full payment. His Chukchee

27.text: neighbors paid nothing. Naturally he was not well contented with his Russian

28.text: origin. One time in my presence he came to the chief official of the Kolyma

29.text: and wanted to enter a petition to the Czar, asking to be released from the

30.text: rank of a Russian creole, and to be lowered to the position of a tributary

31.text: Chukchee. “They pay only one ruble per year,” said he. The chief official

32.text: declared that this was impossible. “Then you would forfeit any right to the

33.text: assistance of the Administration,” added he. “Do not bother me with your

34.text: exactions,” said the poor Russian nomad, “and I will never ask for your

35.text: assistance.” Kasanov married a Chukchee woman according to Chukchee

36.text: rites. He refused to have the Christian rite performed. “Then my children

37.text: would be entered as Russians,” he explained. “I prefer to have them illegal

38.text: and Chukchee, as their mother is.” The whole mode of thought of this man is

39.text: quite Chukchee. Thus he says that if the authorities will continue to be so

40.text: severe on him in the payment of arrears, he will settle the question by

41.text: destroying his own life. All this took place in the year 1895-96. I do not

42.text: know whether Kasanov is still alive.

43.text: Medical Succor. — Medical succor is another branch of official assistance.
